title: Finance Operations Playbook for PE-Backed Companies
summary: PE-backed portfolio company reporting starts the day the deal closes. See what a sponsor expects monthly, and how fast your close actually has to get.
body_markdown:
## What Changes After a Private Equity Investment


PE-backed portfolio company reporting replaces an owner’s reporting habit with a fixed monthly package an institutional investor consumes on a published calendar.


The Association for Financial Professionals describes the change bluntly. Reporting volume “doubles literally overnight,” daily cash tracking becomes normal in the weeks after close, formats go rigid and standardized across the sponsor’s portfolio, and turnaround windows collapse ([AFP, June 29, 2026](https://www.financialprofessionals.org/training-resources/resources/articles/Details/what-pe-firms-look-for-in-portfolio-company-finance-teams) ). Sponsors expect to walk into fragmented systems and no dedicated planning resource. They expect you to meet the portfolio standard anyway. The line worth taping to the wall is the one about liquidity. You cannot hide cash flow.


Six things change at once, usually inside the first reporting period.


- **The accounting basis.** Profitable mid-market companies often run on a tax basis or a modified cash basis, because that’s what the return needed. A sponsor can’t underwrite that, and the credit agreement almost always defines its math by reference to GAAP.
- **The calendar.** A PE sponsor monthly reporting package is typically due inside 10 to 15 business days of month end. That pushes the close itself back to roughly 7 to 10 business days, which for most companies is a week faster than today.
- **The audience.** Three groups now read the same numbers on three deadlines. The sponsor wants value creation. The lender wants covenant math. The tax authorities want a structure that changed on the day the deal closed.
- **Cash.** A rolling 13-week forecast becomes a standing weekly deliverable, reported separately from the income statement and built from expected receipts and disbursements rather than derived from the budget.
- **The board rhythm.** The National Association of Corporate Directors describes the cadence sponsors run: regular CEO calls, monthly business reviews, and quarterly board meetings built for strategic debate with custom KPI dashboards. PE boards typically run 5 to 7 members for agility and expand to 12 or more during major transformations ([NACD, December 10, 2025](https://www.nacdonline.org/all-governance/governance-resources/governance-research/outlook-and-challenges/2026-governance-outlook/unlock-value-through-governance-in-private-equity-portfolio-companies/) ).
- **The diligence file.** The adjusted EBITDA that set the purchase price doesn’t stay in a PDF. It’s the number the sponsor’s model, the lender’s covenant levels, and the management incentive plan were all built on, so it has to be visible in the books.


One more reason to get this right early. Bain and Company puts the average holding period at exit at around seven years, up from five to six across 2010 to 2021, with roughly 32,000 unsold companies representing $3.8 trillion of unrealized value still sitting in portfolios ([Bain and Company, February 22, 2026](https://www.bain.com/insights/outlook-gaining-traction-global-private-equity-report-2026/) ). The system you stand up this quarter is the one you’ll live inside for most of a decade. Build it once.


If you’re comparing this against the other ownership paths a growing company can take, the[finance operations by stage overview](https://www.indinero.com/blog/finance-ops-by-funding-stage-overview/) maps how the same six dimensions behave under different capital structures.


### The First 100 Days After Close


The first 100 days prove three things in sequence. That the opening balance sheet is defensible. That the package lands on time. That cash and covenants are controlled before the first test date.


A first 100 days PE-backed CFO plan breaks into three windows, and the order isn’t negotiable. Skip ahead and you end up rebuilding closed periods.


**Day 1 to 30. A trustworthy opening balance sheet and one validated close.**


- Establish the acquisition-date balance sheet under ASC 805 and reconcile it to the deal’s funds flow. Fees, escrow, debt draw, rollover equity, and seller notes all have to land somewhere.
- Map the old chart of accounts to the sponsor’s standard chart before the first close. Remapping a closed period costs far more than mapping an open one.
- Carry the diligence adjustments into the ledger. For each one, decide whether it’s a permanent booking, a reporting-only add-back, or an item that dies at close.
- Agree the EBITDA definition in writing. There are usually three. GAAP net income rolled up to EBITDA, the sponsor’s adjusted EBITDA from diligence, and the credit agreement’s defined EBITDA with its negotiated add-backs. Name all three, reconcile them, and publish the bridge.


**Day 31 to 60. The package running to a day-10 close target.**


- Put a close calendar in place with named owners and a hard cutoff, then run it twice before you promise it to anyone. A documented[month-end close checklist](https://www.indinero.com/blog/month-end-close-checklist-saas/) is the cheapest version of this.
- Standardize the package. Income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement against budget, written variance commentary on anything material, a margin and EBITDA bridge, and a working capital snapshot.
- Automate the recurring journal entries. The Hackett Group’s research on Digital World Class finance organizations found they run close cycles 35% to 57% shorter than peers and operate at 45% lower cost as a percentage of revenue ([The Hackett Group, June 9, 2025](https://www.thehackettgroup.com/the-hackett-group-digital-world-class-finance-teams-operate-at-45-lower-cost-and-deliver-faster-smarter-insights/) ).
- Clear the four reconciliations that usually block a close. Bank, intercompany, payroll clearing, and deferred revenue.


**Day 61 to 100. Cash forecast, covenant model, and KPI dashboard operational.**


- Stand up the rolling 13-week cash forecast with a weekly variance report against the prior week’s projection.
- Build the covenant model and calculate current headroom. AFP recommends modeling that headroom against both a base case and a 15% to 20% downside, specifically for net debt to EBITDA thresholds, interest coverage ratios, and minimum liquidity requirements.
- Publish the KPI and value creation dashboard, carrying the leading indicators for each initiative rather than only the lagging financials.
- Decide the audit or review path for the first fiscal year end and start the readiness work, because that deadline is set by the credit agreement, not by the auditor’s calendar.


Why day 10, specifically. AFP’s pre-close guidance tells finance teams to compress the monthly close to 7 to 10 business days before the deal closes, rather than discovering the gap once the sponsor’s pace forces it ([AFP, April 28, 2026](https://www.financialprofessionals.org/training-resources/resources/articles/Details/the-90-days-before-a-pe-deal-closes-what-finance-teams-must-do-before-day-1) ). If the package is due on business day 12 and your close finishes on day 14, nothing else here matters yet.


## Service Requirements


A company between $5M and $50M in revenue typically needs six finance services running simultaneously in the first year after close.


The private equity portfolio company reporting requirements that attach to a deal rarely arrive one at a time. They land together, in the same quarter, on the same team.


- **Accrual GAAP close on a fixed calendar.** The deliverable isn’t “financials.” It’s a repeatable close producing the same package, in the same format, by the same business day, every month. A documented calendar with named owners, automated recurring entries, and reconciliations finished before the reporting layer runs are what decide whether it holds.
- **Purchase-accounting support for the opening balance sheet.** Acquisition-date fair value measurement, intangible identification, and two elections covered below that most owners have never had to make.
- **Audit or review readiness, depending on what the documents say.** Also covered below, including the part about who is allowed to sign.
- **Multi-entity consolidation under the holdco.** Sponsors usually hold the business through a holding company, often with a blocker entity and sometimes with the operating company split from a real estate entity the original owner still controls. That’s a consolidation requirement on day one, with intercompany eliminations, management fee allocations, and intercompany loans. The[multi-entity accounting guide](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-entity-accounting-guide/) covers the mechanics.
- **Tax structuring work created by the deal.** If the target was an S corporation and the owner rolled equity, an F reorganization is the common structure, giving the buyer a step-up in asset basis while the rolling owner defers tax on the rolled portion. A Section 338(h)(10) election also delivers a step-up, but it requires a qualified stock purchase of at least 80% of voting power and value, and the rolled portion is generally taxed at close instead. Short-period returns, new registrations, and transaction cost allocation follow, all inside[business tax services](https://www.indinero.com/services/business-tax-services/) .
- **CFO-level support for the sponsor and board cadence.** Someone has to own the narrative, not only the numbers. EY frames the real gap as “the distance between data and decision,” and notes that value creation plans now move in months rather than years ([EY, March 3, 2026](https://www.ey.com/en_us/insights/private-equity/finance-transformations-real-value-in-private-equity) ). That’s the job[CFO services](https://www.indinero.com/services/cfo-services/) are scoped to do.


### Audit or Review Readiness, and Who Is Allowed to Sign It


Most mid-market owners have never had to distinguish a compilation from a review from an audit, and the deal documents assume you can. The AICPA’s own comparison is the clean authority ([AICPA and CIMA, September 30, 2023](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/professional-insights/video/what-is-the-difference-among-a-compilation-review-and-audit) ).


Service Assurance provided What the CPA does Independence required


Compilation None Presents the statements, obtains no assurance, and indicates any lack of independence No


Review Limited assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement Inquiry and analytical procedures Yes


Audit High, but not absolute, assurance Inquiry and analytics, plus understanding internal controls, assessing the risk of material misstatement including fraud risk, and verification procedures Yes


The AICPA’s guidance on when each applies maps almost exactly onto the private equity path. A compilation suits a business seeking lower amounts of financing. A review is usually appropriate as a business grows and seeks larger financing. An audit is typically appropriate, and often required, for complex financing, outside investors, or a sale.


Here’s the part that surprises people. The firm that keeps your books cannot audit or review them. Independence forbids it. The right split is that your accounting team gets the company audit-ready, maintains the schedules an auditor will request, and runs the PBC list, while an independent CPA firm issues the opinion. Plan for two relationships, not one.


### The Opening Balance Sheet and the Pushdown Election


Under ASC 805, every business combination runs through one model, the acquisition method. The acquirer recognizes identifiable assets acquired, liabilities assumed, and any noncontrolling interest at acquisition-date fair value, with the residual recorded as goodwill or as a bargain purchase gain. Third-party valuation work is usually required for customer relationships, trade names, noncompete agreements, and developed technology. The delay is rarely the valuation. It’s assembling what the specialist needs.


Two timing facts decide how much pain arrives later.


- **The measurement period is capped at one year from the acquisition date.** Provisional amounts can be adjusted inside it, and only for new information about facts that existed at closing. It is not a window for second thoughts. FASB’s ASU 2015-16 also changed the mechanics, so a measurement-period adjustment is recognized in the period it’s determined, with the depreciation and amortization effects booked in that same period as if the accounting had been complete at the acquisition date.
- **Pushdown accounting is an option, and it’s irrevocable.** FASB’s ASU 2014-17 gives an acquired company the choice to apply pushdown accounting in its separate financial statements when an acquirer obtains control. The election has to be made before that period’s statements are available to be issued, and once made it can’t be reversed ([FASB, ASU 2014-17](https://storage.fasb.org/ASU%202014-17.pdf) ).


Treat pushdown as a day-30 decision, not a year-end one. It determines whether the operating company’s standalone statements carry the stepped-up basis and the new goodwill, which changes depreciation and amortization, which changes GAAP EBITDA, which can move covenant math if the credit agreement wasn’t drafted to neutralize it.


### The Rolling 13-Week Cash Forecast


This is the one requirement most mid-market finance teams have never built. It’s a direct-method forecast of cash receipts and disbursements, week by week, over a rolling 13-week horizon, rebuilt and reissued every week with a variance report against the prior week’s projection.


AFP’s methodology guidance puts the receipts and disbursements approach, built from actual expected inflows and outflows rather than derived from projected financials, squarely in the short-horizon slot. Its practical rule is worth borrowing: a model that’s 90% reliable and easy to maintain beats one that’s 95% reliable and needs constant modification ([AFP, April 15, 2020](https://www.financialprofessionals.org/training-resources/resources/articles/Details/selecting-a-cash-forecasting-methodology) ).


Why build it before anyone asks. When liquidity tightens, this is the exact format a lender writes into documents. A 2011 amendment to a credit agreement filed by General Maritime Corporation required 13-week cash flow projections delivered weekly during a liquidity waiver period, each including “a variance report describing in reasonable detail the variance(s) in actual cash flow from projected cash flow” ([SEC EDGAR, filed 2011](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1443799/000110465911065189/a11-25839_1ex10d5.htm) ). That’s a stress scenario, not a day-one covenant. The point is that a company already running the format isn’t building one under pressure. If the weekly rebuild is the part you don’t have capacity for, that’s what[outsourced cash flow forecasting](https://www.indinero.com/blog/outsourced-cash-flow-forecasting-services/) is for.


## Compliance Triggers


A private equity investment fires six compliance triggers at once, and most attach on the day the deal closes rather than at year end.


1.


**GAAP conversion.** Fires when the company has been reporting on a tax basis or a modified cash basis. The work is revenue cutoff, receivables and collectibility, payables and accrued expenses, deferred revenue, prepaid expenses, inventory where applicable, and accrued compensation. Every one of those is a balance sheet account that didn’t previously exist, which is why the first accrual close takes longer than a normal month.


2.


**Purchase accounting under ASC 805.** Fires on the acquisition date. The disciplines are acquisition-date fair value measurement, the one-year measurement period, measurement-period adjustments recognized in the period determined, and the irrevocable pushdown election. All covered above.


3.


**An audit or review obligation written into the deal documents.** Fires on signing, not at year end. Read the credit agreement and the equity documents together, because they can impose different levels of assurance on different deadlines. A filed credit agreement exhibit gives the shape of it: unaudited monthly statements within 45 days of month end, unaudited quarterly statements within 45 days of quarter end, and audited annual statements within 90 days of fiscal year end, with a covenant compliance report delivered concurrently and certified by a responsible officer ([SEC EDGAR, Exhibit 10.48, July 1, 2013](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001475274/000119312513293892/d498394dex1048.htm) ). Don’t confuse the fund audit with yours, either. The SEC’s guidance for private fund advisers covers audits of the fund itself by a PCAOB-registered accountant, with statements going to investors within 120 days of the fund’s fiscal year end ([SEC, updated October 31, 2024](https://www.sec.gov/investment/private-fund-advisers) ). That one belongs to the sponsor. Yours comes from the credit agreement, so work the[audit prep checklist](https://www.indinero.com/blog/audit-prep-for-startups-checklist/) against your own deadline.


4.


**Lender covenant reporting.** If the deal carried debt, maintenance covenants are generally tested quarterly, with a compliance certificate delivered alongside the financial statements, typically 45 to 60 days after quarter end, and EBITDA in that calculation is a defined term with negotiated add-backs rather than a GAAP measure ([Sidley Austin, March 24, 2026](https://www.sidley.com/en/insights/newsupdates/2026/03/financial-covenants-in-private-credit-transactions) ). The borrower owns this. The certificate is prepared by the company and signed by a responsible officer, usually the CFO. For ratio construction, cushions, and cure rights in detail, see the deeper treatment of[debt covenant reporting](https://www.indinero.com/blog/finance-ops-series-c-playbook/) .


5.


**Related-party disclosure under ASC 850.** Fires the moment the sponsor starts charging the company. ASC 850-10-50-1 requires disclosure of the nature of the relationship, a description of the transactions, the dollar amounts for each period presented, the effect of any change in how terms are established, and amounts due to or from related parties. The list that gets caught is longer than owners expect. Management and monitoring fees, transaction fees charged at close and again on each add-on, board fees paid to sponsor-affiliated directors, services bought from other companies the sponsor owns, seller notes left in the structure, and rent paid to a real estate entity the original owner still controls. To call any of it arm’s length, you have to substantiate it. A management fee needs a written services agreement with a defined scope and a benchmarked or cost-based rate, not a round number posted monthly with no support.


6.


**Multi-state exposure surfaced in diligence.** Economic nexus after South Dakota v. Wayfair, Inc. doesn’t require an office, employees, or property in a state, and states including California, Massachusetts, and New York assert income tax nexus on revenue thresholds alone. The remediation path is a nexus study followed, where exposure exists, by voluntary disclosure agreements that typically abate penalties and cap the lookback period. Counsel writing on exit readiness makes the timing point directly, noting that a nexus study can identify exposure and allow remediation through voluntary disclosure at far lower cost than the same exposure found in a buyer’s diligence ([National Law Review, June 25, 2026](https://natlawreview.com/article/what-expect-when-youre-expecting-exit-financial-tax-readiness) ). If diligence already found it, the clock is running.


## The Typical Tooling Stack


The tooling question after close isn’t which system is best. It’s which part of your current stack broke first, and whether replacing it belongs in year one or year two.


Things tend to break in a predictable order.


1. **The general ledger, when the holdco structure arrives.** QuickBooks handles one entity well. It handles a holdco, an operating company, a blocker, and a real estate entity badly, and it handles intercompany eliminations and consolidated reporting worse. This is the usual forcing function for a move to NetSuite or Sage Intacct, both of which carry native multi-entity consolidation, currency translation, and automated elimination entries.
2. **Accounts payable, when approval thresholds become real.** Sponsors and lenders both care about spend controls, and Bill.com for AP workflow and approvals is the common landing spot.
3. **Spend and card management, when expense coding has to tie to the new chart of accounts.** Ramp and Brex, paired with policy enforcement rather than after-the-fact coding.
4. **The reporting layer, when the sponsor’s template doesn’t match what the ledger produces.** A consolidation and reporting layer sits on top, so the sponsor package, the lender package, and the management package all come from one source.
5. **Planning, when budget versus actual stops being a spreadsheet exercise.** This is where variance commentary and the 13-week cash forecast live.
6. **Payroll, when multi-state registrations follow the nexus work.** Gusto and equivalents, re-registered state by state.


Automation deserves its own line, because it separates a close you can accelerate from one you can’t. Digital World Class finance organizations automate roughly 99% of journal entries against about 85% for peers, and run with up to 42% fewer full-time equivalents across key finance functions ([The Hackett Group, June 9, 2025](https://www.thehackettgroup.com/the-hackett-group-digital-world-class-finance-teams-operate-at-45-lower-cost-and-deliver-faster-smarter-insights/) ). Recurring entries are where a day-15 close becomes a day-10 close.


Now the sequencing advice most tooling content skips. Don’t attempt an ERP migration during the first 100 days. That window belongs to a defensible opening balance sheet and a reliable close on the system you already have, and a cutover in month two puts both at risk. Run the selection in parallel and cut over at a clean fiscal boundary once the close is stable. Stabilize the close first.


One practical note on providers. Indinero works inside the stack you already run, including QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, Sage Intacct, Bill.com, Ramp, Brex, and Gusto, with no proprietary platform to migrate onto. That matters here, because your sponsor may standardize the portfolio on something else in year three and you shouldn’t have to change[accounting services](https://www.indinero.com/services/accounting-services/) providers to follow.


## Common Mistakes at This Stage


The expensive mistakes in finance operations after a private equity investment are calendar errors, credibility errors, and scope errors. Not accounting errors.


Each one below compounds across a hold period that now averages about seven years.


1. **Treating the sponsor package as a chore bolted onto the close.** If the package is something the team assembles after the close finishes, it will always be late. The due date has to drive the close calendar backwards. The symptom is familiar. The close “finishes” on business day 12 and the package goes out on day 18.
2. **Missing the deadline in month one.** The first package sets the tone for the whole hold period. A sponsor who receives a late, reconciled-after-the-fact first package starts asking different questions, and the team spends four quarters earning back credibility it could have simply kept.
3. **Leaving the diligence adjustments out of the books.** The sponsor underwrote adjusted EBITDA from the quality-of-earnings report and the lender set covenant levels off a related number. If the ledger never reflects those decisions, every variance review turns into a reconciliation argument. The fix is a standing EBITDA bridge, from GAAP net income to sponsor adjusted EBITDA to credit agreement EBITDA, published every month.
4. **Under-resourcing the opening balance sheet.** It gets built once, is audited against for years, and sets the depreciation and amortization flowing through every future period. Skipping the intangible valuation work, or letting the one-year measurement period lapse with provisional amounts unresolved, creates problems that surface at the first audit and again at exit.
5. **Discovering a covenant definition after the first test date.** Companies that calculate compliance using GAAP EBITDA, or using the diligence number, can be wrong in either direction. Build the model from the credit agreement’s own definitions inside the first 60 days and test it against a real quarter before the certificate is due.
6. **Writing a board pack full of operations and no strategy.** NACD’s survey of private company directors found 45% say packs are overly focused on operations at the expense of strategy, 39% say they’re too internally focused to give any read on the wider market, and 39% say risk reporting is missing ([NACD Directorship, October 2, 2024](https://www.nacdonline.org/all-governance/governance-resources/directorship-magazine/online-exclusives/2024/q4-2024/private-company-boards-need-additional-information-and-time-to-enable-strategic-discussion-survey-finds/) ). In the same research, only about 53% rated their packs very or extremely effective overall ([NACD, July 25, 2024](https://www.nacdonline.org/all-governance/governance-resources/governance-surveys/surveys-benchmarking/2024-private-company-board-practices-and-oversight-survey/board-reporting/) ). A month-end binder is not a board pack.
7. **Assuming the firm that files the return can also audit the books.** Independence forbids it for audits and reviews, and the same rule applies to an outsourced accounting provider. Two relationships, not one.
8. **Building the whole function in-house because the sponsor expects rigor.** Some of this work is continuous and some is episodic, and hiring for the episodic parts is how a $20M company ends up with an idle technical accountant. Run the[in-house versus outsourced accounting](https://www.indinero.com/blog/outsourced-accounting-vs-in-house/) comparison before you post the job.


## What’s Coming Next: Add-On and Exit Triggers


Two events reset the finance function again after the first 100 days. The first add-on acquisition, and exit preparation.


**The add-on trigger.** Sponsors in the lower middle market buy more often than they build, so across a hold period averaging about seven years, a platform company should plan for at least one acquisition rather than treat it as a possibility. When the first one closes, several things change together.


- A second ASC 805 purchase price allocation and a second opening balance sheet, each with its own one-year measurement period.
- Chart of accounts mapping for the acquired entity, done before the first combined close rather than after.
- Intercompany eliminations and a real[consolidation process](https://www.indinero.com/blog/multi-entity-consolidation-process/) , not a spreadsheet roll-up.
- A combined close calendar, which usually means the acquired company’s close has to speed up to match the platform’s deadline.
- KPI standardization, so the sponsor can see organic performance separately from acquired performance. Exit buyers insist on that separation too.
- Working capital normalization across entities with different payment terms, and an expanded state tax footprint, because the acquired company brings its own nexus and registrations.


**The exit trigger.** Serious exit preparation starts eighteen to twenty-four months before a sale process launches, not when the banker is hired. The cornerstone is consolidated audited financial statements incorporating all add-on acquisitions, prepared under GAAP, and the timeline for clean audit opinions should not be underestimated where acquired businesses had different levels of reporting sophistication. On the sell-side quality of earnings, overly aggressive or poorly documented adjustments erode credibility and can result in purchase price reductions ([National Law Review, June 25, 2026](https://natlawreview.com/article/what-expect-when-youre-expecting-exit-financial-tax-readiness) ). Build a normalized working capital target that accounts for differences across acquisitions, before a post-closing dispute finds it for you.


Governance follows the same curve. NACD notes that committees typically increase in formality as portfolio companies approach exit, and that companies with formal board structures and independent oversight get flagged by buyers as investment-ready.


One scope boundary to set now rather than later. The sell-side quality-of-earnings report and the audit opinion both require an independent firm. Name them in the plan, budget them separately, and route them out.

## Frequently asked questions


These come up in the first two quarters after close, usually in this order. What a sponsor actually wants in the monthly package, how fast the close has to get, whether accrual GAAP is really mandatory, what the 13-week forecast does that the budget doesn’t, who signs the covenant certificate, and what changes when the first add-on lands. The answers below are short on purpose.


### What does a private equity sponsor expect in the monthly reporting package?


A private equity sponsor expects accrual GAAP income statement, balance sheet, and cash flow statement against budget, with written variance commentary on material items. Most packages also carry a margin and EBITDA bridge, a working capital snapshot, covenant compliance math where the deal carries debt, and a KPI dashboard. It’s due within 10 to 15 business days of month end, in the sponsor’s format, which is why indinero builds the package out of the close rather than after it.


### How fast does a PE-backed company have to close its books?


A PE-backed company typically closes its books in 7 to 10 business days, because the sponsor package is due within 10 to 15. The Association for Financial Professionals recommends compressing the close to that range before the deal closes, not after the sponsor’s pace exposes the gap. Automating recurring journal entries and clearing the bank, intercompany, payroll clearing, and deferred revenue reconciliations early is what usually turns a day-15 close into the day-10 close indinero runs for sponsor-backed clients.


### Does a private equity investment force a move to full accrual GAAP reporting?


Yes, in practice a private equity investment moves the company to full accrual GAAP, because both the sponsor and the credit agreement require it. The sponsor needs accrual GAAP to compare performance across its holdings and tie results to the model it underwrote, and the credit agreement almost always defines covenant math by reference to GAAP. Converting from a tax or modified cash basis means building receivables, accrued expenses, deferred revenue, prepaids, and accrued compensation from scratch, and that conversion sits inside indinero’s accounting and GAAP close scope.


### What does a 13-week cash forecast do that the annual budget does not?


A 13-week cash forecast answers whether cash will be in the bank on a specific Friday, which an annual accrual budget never does. It’s built with the direct method from expected receipts and disbursements rather than derived from projected financials, and it’s rebuilt every week with a variance report against the prior week’s projection. That weekly rebuild catches payroll timing, debt service, and covenant pressure early, and it’s part of the fractional CFO scope indinero runs alongside the close.


### Who owns covenant reporting when the deal is financed with debt?


The company owns covenant reporting as the borrower, preparing the compliance certificate that a responsible officer, usually the CFO, signs and certifies. The lender verifies and the sponsor monitors, but neither takes the obligation off the company. Maintenance covenants are generally tested quarterly, with the certificate delivered alongside the financial statements, typically 45 to 60 days after quarter end, and indinero’s fractional CFO support builds the model behind it.


### How does reporting change once the sponsor buys an add-on?


An add-on turns a single-entity close into a consolidation, adding a second ASC 805 purchase price allocation and a second opening balance sheet. The acquired entity’s chart of accounts has to be mapped before the first combined close, intercompany eliminations become real, and the acquired company’s close usually has to speed up to the platform’s deadline. KPIs get standardized so organic performance stays separable, and the state tax footprint expands, which is why indinero’s scope widens instead of requiring a new vendor search.


### Can an outsourced finance team meet sponsor reporting standards?


Yes, an outsourced finance team can meet sponsor reporting standards when it runs to the sponsor’s calendar, chart of accounts, and template. Scope matters as much as speed, so purchase accounting support, multi-entity consolidation, related-party disclosure, and post-recapitalization tax have to sit inside the engagement, which is how indinero structures it. Indinero does not perform audits, reviews, or quality-of-earnings reports, because independence bars the firm that keeps the books from attesting to them, so an independent CPA firm issues the opinion while indinero runs audit readiness.
